one_liner: Abandoned Rust ClickHouse-protocol server on forked DataFusion; 3.1x faster than ClickHouse on plain sum, 6.7x slower on group-by.
what_it_does: TensorBase is a standalone columnar SQL server that speaks the ClickHouse native TCP protocol (default port 9528), so you connect with the stock clickhouse-client or a ClickHouse driver and create tables with ENGINE = BaseStorage. It supports a small subset of ClickHouse SQL: integer, float, Date, DateTime, Decimal, String, FixedString and UUID columns; count/sum/avg/min/max; some toYear-style date functions; full-row INSERT (VALUES, FORMAT CSV, INSERT ... SELECT); and remote() tables that point at ClickHouse or MySQL servers. It is not a drop-in ClickHouse replacement and has no library API for embedding.
how_it_is_fast: Storage is a no-LSM 'partition tree': each (table, column, partition-key) pair is one append-only, unsorted, uncompressed flat file, and inserts are routed by a partition-key expression JIT-compiled with Cranelift (the basejit crate), then written with fallocate + pwrite at an offset reserved atomically in sled, with no sorting, merging or compaction. At query time every matching column-partition file is mmapped read-only and wrapped zero-copy as an unowned Arrow Buffer; the buffers are registered as a DataFusion MemTable, and the raw SQL runs on a vendored fork of Arrow-DataFusion 6.0 built with the packed_simd 'simd' feature. The sum win most likely comes from scanning raw arrays already in the page cache with no decompression, and the project does not explain why group-by is slow.
when_to_use: Learning or borrowing code: a compact Rust example of a ClickHouse native-protocol server (plus a MySQL-protocol one) sitting on Arrow and DataFusion.
Studying zero-copy storage: mmap'd flat column files handed straight to Arrow/DataFusion as unowned buffers, with JIT-compiled partition routing.
Throwaway experiments with full-scan sum/count/min/max over a few numeric columns that fit in RAM, driven from an existing clickhouse-client workflow.
Append-only bulk loads into a scratch store where losing recent writes after a crash is acceptable.
when_not_to_use: Anything in production. The README itself recommends ClickHouse for production, says no new features are planned, and the code has not changed since December 2021.

GROUP BY or anything beyond a simple aggregate. Its own benchmark is 6.7x slower than ClickHouse on a year group-by count, the TPC-H page says performance 'has not been tuned' (only a modified Q1 at SF1 is shown), and the authors describe it as 'soon slower in more complex cases'.
Data bigger than RAM or read from cold disk. Column files are stored uncompressed, and the benchmark notes say ClickHouse wins from a cold disk because of compression.
Workloads that need durability or crash safety. The write path I read calls fallocate, pwrite and close, ignores their return codes, and never fsyncs. There is no WAL.

ClickHouse schemas that use Enum8 (#114), partial-column INSERT, db.table references in the engine (#106), or string literals (#230, 'select 'abc'' returns nothing). Any feature past the short list in docs/lang.md is missing.

integration.form: Standalone server binary: Linux release zips up to v2021.07.05, or built with cargo from the workspace. There are two binaries, server (ClickHouse protocol) and mysql_server. It is not packaged as an embeddable library.
integration.dependencies: Vendored forks of arrow 6.4, datafusion 6.0 and parquet; sled 0.34 for metadata and partition bookkeeping; tokio 1.x; tikv-jemallocator; lzzzz (LZ4, wire compression); clickhouse-rs-cityhash-sys; the mysql 21 crate; and two git-branch dependencies, tensorbase/basejit (Cranelift 0.69 expression JIT, no license file in the repo) and tensorbase/baselog.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly-2021-12-17, pinned in rust-toolchain. The docs say nightly is required. Stable Rust is not supported.
integration.platforms: Linux (also Windows via WSL2, VMs or Docker). docs/docs.md says macOS is not supported and that CPUs other than x86-64 are 'not tested', although a blog post reports a demo run on RISC-V hardware. CI runs only on ubuntu-20.04.
integration.thread_safety: As a server, it accepts concurrent client connections on a tokio runtime, and the docs advertise highly concurrent ingestion. Inserts into tables with String columns take a per-table spin lock implemented as a sled compare-and-swap. Isolation and consistency semantics for concurrent reads and writes are not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — clickhouse-client and ClickHouse native drivers connect unchanged, but only a small subset of ClickHouse SQL and types is implemented, tables must use ENGINE = BaseStorage, and there is no MergeTree ordering, compression or replication.

gotchas: The headline '5x~10000x faster than ClickHouse' numbers belong to the closed TensorBase Frontier Edition, not this repo. On HN, a commenter (zX41ZdbW) noted that the synthetic system.numbers queries compile into a loop the compiler removes entirely, so no data is processed.

Every query mmaps every matching column-partition file, and the mappings appear never to be released: QueryState's Drop impl is commented out, and GitHub code search finds no caller of mm_unmap. Expect virtual address space to grow on a long-running server.

Large result sets can hang the client. #86 (open): SELECT on a string column without LIMIT times out because the server does not split big Arrow RecordBatches into smaller blocks. An INSERT block that spans 1000 or more partition-key values is rejected with TooManyPartsPerBlock.
The runtime depends on github.com/tensorbase/basejit by git branch. That repo has no LICENSE file, so check licensing before you redistribute a build, even though TensorBase itself is Apache-2.0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only as reference code for putting a ClickHouse wire-protocol front end on DataFusion. Otherwise use upstream Apache DataFusion (maintained and far newer than TensorBase's pinned 2021 fork) for an embeddable Rust engine, StarRocks, Apache Doris or QuestDB for a maintained server that beats ClickHouse on its own benchmarks, or chDB for ClickHouse SQL inside a process.
verified_claims_summary: The repo's first-party table (docs/benchmarks.md, committed 2021-04-20, before the December 2021 DataFusion 6.0 upgrade; no scripts or compiler flags, release profile uses thin LTO) covers a 1.46B-row, two-column NYC Taxi table held in memory, best of 3 runs, on a 1-socket Xeon Platinum 8260 (24 cores / 48 threads, 192 GB DDR4-2400): TensorBase's April-2021 main branch ran sum(trip_id) in 0.079 s vs ClickHouse v21.2.5.5 at 0.248 s (3.1x faster), but a year group-by count took 3.375 s vs 0.514 s (about 6.7x slower). The README's '2x faster write throughput' has no published numbers (the blog says only that it was 'found in the Rust driver based bench' with the bottleneck 'at the client side', and the in-repo ingestion bench compares raw appends against a ClickHouse MergeTree table that sorts and compresses on insert), and the README's 'benchmarked against ClickHouse 2021.6' contradicts the table's v21.2.5.5.
status_note: Abandoned: code changes stopped in December 2021, the last commit (2022-05-10) only disabled dependabot, the last binary release is v2021.07.05 and 48 issues are open; it is Apache-2.0 with about 1.5k stars, but the pinned 2021 nightly toolchain and a git dependency with no license file make it reading material rather than something to vendor.
